animals.blurb: One of the most recognizable songbirds, males sport brilliant red plumage while females are warm brown with red accents. They are non-migratory and sing year-round.
animals.hint: A brilliant red songbird with a pointed crest

animals.blurb: Bold and intelligent, blue jays are known for their striking blue plumage and loud, jay! calls. They can mimic hawk calls and are important oak tree planters.
animals.hint: A crested blue bird with bold white and black markings

animals.blurb: A beloved harbinger of spring, robins are famous for their cheery song and habit of pulling earthworms from lawns. Their blue eggs are iconic.
animals.hint: An orange-breasted bird famous for hunting worms on lawns

animals.habitat: Open country, woodlands, deserts, urban areas
animals.blurb: The most common hawk in North America, often seen soaring on thermals or perched on telephone poles. Their distinctive scream is Hollywood's go-to raptor call.
animals.hint: A soaring raptor with a rusty-red tail

animals.habitat: Near large bodies of water, coastal areas
animals.blurb: America's national bird, bald eagles made a remarkable recovery from near-extinction due to DDT. They build the largest nests of any North American bird.
animals.hint: The iconic white-headed symbol of America

animals.blurb: The most widespread owl in the Americas, nicknamed the 'tiger of the sky.' They hunt everything from mice to skunks and are one of the few predators of porcupines.
animals.hint: A powerful owl with distinctive ear tufts

animals.blurb: A small owl with excellent camouflage that comes in red and gray color morphs. Their eerie, whinnying call is often heard at night but rarely seen.
animals.hint: A small, camouflaged owl with a whinnying call

animals.blurb: Known for its distinctive 'Who cooks for you?' call, the barred owl has dark eyes unlike most owls. They have expanded westward into spotted owl territory.
animals.hint: A round-headed owl asking 'Who cooks for you?'

animals.blurb: The only breeding hummingbird in eastern North America, males flash an iridescent ruby throat. They can fly backwards and beat their wings 53 times per second.
animals.hint: A tiny hovering jewel with a glittering red throat

animals.blurb: One of the few hummingbirds to remain in the US year-round, males perform spectacular dive displays, reaching speeds of 60 mph. Their rose-red crown sparkles in sunlight.
animals.hint: A western hummingbird with a rosy head

animals.habitat: Ponds, lakes, rivers, marshes, urban parks
animals.blurb: The most familiar duck in the Northern Hemisphere, and ancestor to most domestic ducks. Males sport an iridescent green head while females are mottled brown.
animals.hint: The classic duck with a metallic green head

animals.blurb: Famous for their V-formation flights and honking calls, Canada geese have adapted remarkably well to urban environments. They mate for life.
animals.hint: A large goose with a black neck and white chinstrap

animals.blurb: The largest heron in North America, standing up to 4.5 feet tall. Patient hunters, they stand motionless before striking fish with lightning speed.
animals.hint: A tall, blue-gray wader that hunts with patience

animals.blurb: Nearly extinct in the early 1900s, wild turkeys have made an incredible comeback. Males display impressive fan-shaped tails and colorful wattles to attract females.
animals.hint: A large ground bird with an iridescent fan tail

animals.blurb: Among the most intelligent birds, crows can use tools, recognize human faces, and hold grudges. They gather in massive winter roosts of thousands of individuals.
animals.hint: An intelligent all-black bird that never forgets a face

animals.blurb: Larger and more intelligent than crows, ravens are master aerial acrobats that tumble through the sky for fun. Their deep, croaking calls echo through wild places.
animals.hint: A large, intelligent black bird with a wedge-shaped tail

animals.blurb: Introduced from Europe in the 1850s, house sparrows are now one of the most widespread birds globally. They are resourceful city dwellers.
animals.hint: A small, chunky brown bird common around buildings

animals.blurb: Introduced to North America by someone who wanted all Shakespeare-mentioned birds in Central Park, starlings form spectacular murmurations of thousands of birds.
animals.hint: An iridescent, speckled bird that moves in stunning flocks

animals.blurb: Named for their mournful cooing, these graceful doves are among the most abundant birds in North America. Their wings make a distinctive whistling sound in flight.
animals.hint: A slender dove with a mournful cooing song

animals.blurb: The familiar city pigeon descended from domesticated rock doves brought to North America in the 1600s. They navigate using Earth's magnetic field and can fly home from hundreds of miles away.
animals.hint: The ubiquitous city bird with iridescent neck feathers

animals.blurb: The smallest woodpecker in North America, often seen at backyard feeders. Their small size allows them to access food sources larger woodpeckers cannot reach.
animals.hint: A small black-and-white woodpecker at your feeder

animals.blurb: Despite its name, the red belly is hard to see—the bright red head stripe is more noticeable. They cache food by wedging it into bark crevices.
animals.hint: A zebra-backed woodpecker with a red head stripe

animals.blurb: The largest woodpecker in North America (excluding the possibly extinct ivory-billed), their rectangular excavations in trees are unmistakable. Inspiration for Woody Woodpecker.
animals.hint: A crow-sized woodpecker with a flaming red crest

animals.blurb: Unlike most woodpeckers, flickers spend much of their time on the ground eating ants. Eastern birds flash yellow under their wings; western birds show salmon-red.
animals.hint: A spotted woodpecker that feeds on ants

animals.blurb: Males transform from drab olive to brilliant yellow each spring. They are strict vegetarians and even feed their young regurgitated seeds rather than insects.
animals.hint: A bright yellow finch that bounces through the air

animals.blurb: Originally from the Southwest, house finches were released in New York in 1940 and spread across the continent. Males vary from pale yellow to deep red depending on diet.
animals.hint: A red-headed finch common at backyard feeders

animals.blurb: Called 'snowbirds' because they arrive in many regions with winter, juncos flash white outer tail feathers as they fly. Regional forms vary greatly in color.
animals.hint: A slate-gray snowbird with white tail edges

animals.blurb: One of the most thoroughly studied birds in North America, song sparrows have highly variable plumage across their range. Each male learns about 10 different songs.
animals.hint: A streaky sparrow with a distinctive breast spot

animals.blurb: Their pure, whistled song sounds like 'Oh Sweet Canada, Canada, Canada.' They come in two color morphs that preferentially mate with each other.
animals.hint: A sparrow with yellow lores singing about Canada

animals.blurb: Males flash brilliant red and yellow shoulder patches while singing their distinctive 'conk-la-ree!' from cattail perches. One of the most abundant birds in North America.
animals.hint: A blackbird with flashy red shoulder patches

animals.blurb: Named for their colors matching Lord Baltimore's coat of arms, these orioles weave remarkable hanging pouch nests. They are fond of orange halves and grape jelly.
animals.hint: A flame-orange songbird that weaves hanging nests

animals.habitat: Open areas, marshes, urban parks, farms
animals.blurb: Their iridescent plumage shimmers with purples, greens, and bronze in sunlight. They walk with a distinctive strut and form enormous flocks in fall.
animals.hint: A glossy blackbird with piercing yellow eyes

animals.blurb: Brood parasites that lay eggs in other birds' nests, cowbirds have been recorded parasitizing over 200 species. Originally they followed bison herds, hence their name.
animals.hint: A chunky blackbird that tricks other birds into raising its young

animals.blurb: Elegant birds with silky plumage, a bandit mask, and waxy red wing tips. They travel in flocks and are so berry-obsessed they sometimes become intoxicated on fermented fruit.
animals.hint: A sleek, crested bird with a yellow tail tip

animals.blurb: These bold little birds are named for their 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' call. They can remember thousands of food-caching locations and their brain neurons are replaced seasonally.
animals.hint: A tiny acrobat with a black cap singing its name

animals.blurb: A perky gray bird with a crest and big black eyes. Their loud 'peter-peter-peter' call rings through winter woods. They pluck fur from live animals to line their nests.
animals.hint: A crested gray bird calling 'peter-peter-peter'

animals.blurb: Unique among birds for walking headfirst down tree trunks, nuthatches can spot insects other birds miss. They wedge seeds into bark and hammer them open.
animals.hint: A tree-walking bird that goes headfirst down trunks

animals.blurb: A loud singer for its size, the Carolina wren's 'teakettle-teakettle-teakettle' is unmistakable. They nest in unusual places like flowerpots, mailboxes, and coat pockets.
animals.hint: A rusty wren with a bold white eyebrow

animals.blurb: Plain but exuberant, house wrens pour out bubbly songs all day long. Males build multiple 'dummy' nests to attract females, who choose and finish one.
animals.hint: A small, plain brown bird with a bubbly song

animals.blurb: Once declining due to nest box competition, bluebirds have recovered thanks to trail networks of nest boxes. Males sport vivid blue backs and rusty breasts.
animals.hint: A brilliant blue thrush with a warm orange breast

animals.blurb: Master mimics that can learn over 200 songs, including car alarms and cell phone rings. They sing day and night, especially unmarried males under a full moon.
animals.hint: A gray songster that mimics everything it hears

animals.blurb: Named for their distinctive cat-like mewing call, catbirds are secretive mimic thrushes. They destroy cowbird eggs laid in their nests, one of few species that do.
animals.hint: A slate-gray bird that mews like a cat

animals.blurb: This rufous-colored bird has the largest song repertoire of any North American bird, with over 1,000 documented songs. They repeat phrases twice.
animals.hint: A rusty bird with the largest song library

animals.habitat: Open fields, parking lots, rooftops, shores
animals.blurb: Famous for their 'broken-wing' display to lure predators from their ground nests. Their loud 'kill-deer' call gives them their name. They nest on gravel rooftops and parking lots.
animals.hint: A plover with double breast bands and a dramatic act

animals.blurb: These plump, camouflaged shorebirds live in forests and probe for earthworms with their flexible-tipped bills. Males perform spectacular sky dances at dusk in spring.
animals.hint: A forest shorebird with a long bill and sky dance

animals.blurb: The most common inland gull, recognized by the black ring around its yellow bill. They thrive in urban environments, especially parking lots and fast-food restaurants.
animals.hint: The parking lot gull with a ringed bill

animals.blurb: Large, familiar coastal gulls that take four years to reach adult plumage. They drop shellfish onto rocks to break them open and are bold scavengers.
animals.hint: A large coastal gull with pink legs

animals.blurb: Distinctive birds with shaggy crests and rattling calls, kingfishers hover and plunge headfirst for fish. Unusually, females are more colorful than males.
animals.hint: A crested fisher with a rattling call

animals.blurb: Nature's cleanup crew, turkey vultures locate carrion by smell—a rare ability among birds. They rock side-to-side in flight on their long, upswept wings.
animals.hint: A dark soarer with a bald red head

animals.blurb: Expanding northward, black vultures are more aggressive than turkey vultures and often displace them from carcasses. They soar on flat wings with white wingtips.
animals.hint: A dark scavenger with silvery wing patches

animals.blurb: Specialized fish-eating raptors that plunge feet-first into water. Their reversible outer toe and spiny foot pads help grip slippery prey. They build huge stick nests.
animals.hint: A fish hawk that dives feet-first

animals.blurb: Agile woodland hawks that specialize in catching birds, often hunting at backyard feeders. They fly fast through dense cover with quick wingbeats and long tails.
animals.hint: A swift woodland hawk that hunts birds

animals.blurb: North America's smallest falcon, about the size of a robin. They hover in place while hunting and nest in tree cavities. Both sexes have striking plumage.
animals.hint: A tiny, colorful falcon that hovers while hunting

animals.blurb: The fastest animal on Earth, stooping at over 200 mph to strike prey in mid-air. They recovered from DDT-induced near-extinction and now thrive on city skyscrapers.
animals.hint: The world's fastest animal, diving from above

animals.blurb: Tall and elegant, great egrets were hunted nearly to extinction for their breeding plumes. Their recovery inspired the Audubon Society, which uses them as their symbol.
animals.hint: A tall, pure white wader with a yellow bill

animals.blurb: Small, stocky herons that are one of the few tool-using birds—they drop insects or bread on the water to lure fish. They stretch their necks surprisingly long when striking.
animals.hint: A small heron that fishes with bait

animals.blurb: Often called the most beautiful duck in North America, males have iridescent green heads with white stripes. They nest in tree cavities and ducklings jump from nest boxes the day after hatching.
animals.hint: A dazzling duck with an iridescent helmet head
